grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The region's finest, fermented dry in the classic style: lime, stone, steel and a long life, from granite and sandstone above all.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Deep gold, low in acid, heady with lychee, rose and ginger; richest on marl and limestone, and the natural Vendanges Tardives grape.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Pinot Gris here, once sold as Tokay d'Alsace: broad, smoky, orchard-fruited and often carrying a little sugar.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains and Muscat Ottonel: smells of the grape itself and finishes dry; the asparagus wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: With Auxerrois, the everyday white and the backbone of Crémant d'Alsace.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.styles: Softer and lower in acid than Pinot Blanc, with which it is usually blended and often labelled.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: Spelt Sylvaner here: light, earthy and dry, admitted to one Grand Cru, Zotzenberg.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The one black grape, once pale and light, now riper; admitted to Grand Cru at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr from the 2022 vintage and at Vorbourg from 2024.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Permitted in Crémant d'Alsace only, never in a still Alsace white.

law.classification: Three appellations covered the region until 2011, when each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own and the count rose to fifty-three: AOC Alsace (1962), the fifty-one Alsace Grand Cru appellations (a tier created in 1975 with Schlossberg as its first site, completed by Kaefferkopf in 2007) and Crémant d'Alsace (1976). Below Grand Cru the 2011 rules also recognised communal denominations such as Côte de Rouffach or Ottrott and named lieux-dits, each with lower yields and higher ripeness than plain Alsace. Grand Cru wine must come from one of the four noble grapes, with exceptions written into a site's own rules: Sylvaner at Zotzenberg, blends at Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf, and Pinot Noir at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr from the 2022 vintage and Vorbourg from 2024. Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles, defined in 1984, are label mentions limited to the noble four. A Premier Cru tier proposed by the growers was still before the appellation authorities when this was written.

tiers: Alsace AOC
The regional appellation, 1962; labels by grape, 100 per cent of the named variety, bottled in the region in the flûte.
Alsace communal and lieu-dit
Since 2011 a village or named site may be added to Alsace, with lower yields and higher minimum ripeness.
Alsace Grand Cru
Fifty-one named sites, each its own appellation since 2011; noble grapes only with a few written exceptions; a vintage is compulsory.
Crémant d'Alsace
Traditional-method sparkling, 1976; Pinot Blanc leads, Chardonnay is allowed here only, rosé is Pinot Noir alone.
Vendanges Tardives
Late harvest of a noble grape at a set minimum sugar, chaptalisation forbidden; may finish dry or sweet.
Sélection de Grains Nobles
Botrytised selection of a noble grape at a higher minimum; always sweet.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained high on wires, higher than in most of France, to keep the fruit above the cold air that pools on the plain and to shade heavy bunches in a sunny year. Grand Cru sites are held to lower yields than plain Alsace and must carry a vintage; many growers in the Haut-Rhin farm organically or biodynamically, a movement that took root here early. Harvest runs long, from early September for the Crémant base through October for the noble grapes, with Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles picked last, by hand, declared in advance and checked by the authorities. Minimum must weights for those two categories are set by grape: 235 grams of sugar per litre for Riesling and Muscat Vendanges Tardives and 257 for Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, rising to 276 and 306 for Sélection de Grains Nobles, with chaptalisation forbidden for both. Hail and spring frost are the old hazards; drought on the thin granite soils is the newer one.
made.winemaking: The classic cellar is simple and reductive: whole-bunch pressing, a cool fermentation in stainless steel or in the large old oval casks, the foudres, that line Alsace cellars and give no oak flavour, then early bottling to keep the aromatics. Malolactic conversion is usually avoided in Riesling and the aromatic grapes to hold acidity. The argument of the last thirty years has been sweetness: some houses ferment everything dry, others stop fermentation and leave sugar in Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, so since the 2021 vintage AOC Alsace whites outside the two late-harvest categories must declare their level on the label, as sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux or on a printed scale. Crémant d'Alsace is made by the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle, at least nine months on the lees and twelve months from tirage before sale. Riesling must be entirely Riesling, but Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois; do not apply one blanket varietal rule. The appellation requires regional bottling, with the flûte prescribed for its still whites.

terroir.climate: Semi-continental, dry and sunny: the Vosges force Atlantic weather to drop its rain on the western side, so Colmar is among the driest towns in France at roughly 500 to 600 millimetres a year. Long, warm, dry autumns let aromatic grapes hang late, which is why the sweet categories are possible and rot is rare. Winters are cold and spring frost threatens the plain more than the slopes.
terroir.soils: A mosaic unlike any other French region: the Rhine rift shattered the ground, so granite, gneiss, schist, volcanic rock, sandstone, limestone, marl and clay all appear within a few kilometres. Granite crus such as Schlossberg and Brand sit at the mouths of valleys; the Rangen above Thann is volcanic; Kastelberg is schist; most of the lower foothills are limestone and marl, the richest ground for Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris.
terroir.topography: The vineyards sit on the foothill shelf between the forested Vosges and the flat Rhine plain, mostly at 200 to 400 metres, on slopes facing east and south-east into the morning sun. The steepest Grand Cru sites climb above the villages; the plain below carries the everyday wines. Colmar and Rouffach lie in the driest pocket behind the highest peaks.
terroir.water: The Rhine flows north along the German border some 20 kilometres east of the vines and the Ill runs parallel through the plain; neither touches the vineyard directly, and the climate owes more to the mountains than to the rivers.

traps: Pinot Blanc is important but not noble: no Grand Cru, no Vendanges Tardives.
Vendanges Tardives may finish nearly dry; Sélection de Grains Nobles is always sweet.
Check sweetness before recommending either Alsace Riesling or German Kabinett; neither name alone establishes the sweetness of every bottle.
Tokay d'Alsace was Pinot Gris; the name was retired by 2007 to protect Hungary's Tokaj.
Chardonnay is legal in Crémant d'Alsace and nowhere else in the appellation.
A Grand Cru that names no grape is a permitted blend, Altenberg de Bergheim or Kaefferkopf, not a mistake.
Edelzwicker and Gentil are both blends; Gentil is the stricter term.
Muscat here is dry; never promise a guest a sweet Muscat as in the Rhône or Roussillon.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Nearly the whole vineyard: cherry, raspberry and violet, light tannin and bright acid, from carbonic Nouveau to cru wines that age like Burgundy.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The grape of Beaujolais Blanc, grown mostly in the north near the Mâconnais border.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Long allowed as a small accessory share in the red and little seen; Beaujolais is Gamay's region, not Pinot's.

law.classification: Three tiers, all under Gamay. Beaujolais AOC covers the whole region, its heart the clay and limestone of the south; Beaujolais-Villages takes in the granite hamlets of the north that sit outside the crus; and the ten crus, Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly and Brouilly, each has its own appellation and need not print the word Beaujolais. Nouveau and Primeur may be made as Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages, never as a cru. The region sits in the Rhône département for the most part, with Saint-Amour across the line in Saône-et-Loire, and in law it belongs to greater Burgundy, so a cru's Gamay may be sold as Bourgogne Gamay.
labels: Wine released the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.
The famous schist hill of Morgon, named on labels as a climat.
Old vines, unregulated, common on the crus.

tiers: Beaujolais
The regional base: red from Gamay, white from Chardonnay, a little rosé; Nouveau is sold at this tier.
Beaujolais-Villages

made.viticulture: Gamay was banished from the Côte d'Or by a ducal edict of 1395 and found its true home on this granite, where its vigour is checked by poor sandy soil. The traditional training is the gobelet, a free-standing bush that suits the warm slopes and the hand picking that whole-bunch fermentation demands; cordon and Guyot are now also permitted. Vine density is high, at least six thousand to the hectare, and yields are capped more tightly for the crus than for Villages and plain Beaujolais. Harvest comes early for Burgundy, late August into September, and the whole region picks fast because Nouveau must be in bottle within weeks. Hail is the enemy of the hillside crus, and the sandy soils drain so quickly that drought now matters more than rot. A growing number of estates farm organically, and the old gobelet vines of Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent are the source of the region's longest-lived wines.
made.winemaking: Whole bunches go uncrushed into a vat that is sealed and often filled with carbon dioxide. In full carbonic maceration the berries ferment from the inside, without yeast contact, producing little tannin and the banana and bubblegum esters of Nouveau; the grapes are pressed after a few days and the juice finishes fermenting off the skins. Semi-carbonic is the norm: the bottom of the vat crushes under its own weight and ferments conventionally, releasing the gas that protects the intact berries above. The crus are increasingly made like red Burgundy, destemmed or whole-bunch with a longer maceration, punched down and aged in older oak foudres or barrels so they gain structure and keep. A natural-wine school rooted in Morgon in the 1980s revived long, cool whole-bunch ferments with native yeasts and little or no added sulphur, and its influence runs through the crus today. Beaujolais Blanc is made as a simple unoaked Chardonnay.

places.name: Beaujolais-Villages
places.note: The granite hamlets of the north outside the ten crus, riper and firmer than plain Beaujolais; the middle tier and a sound bistro pour.

places.name: The ten crus
places.note: All on the granite and schist north of Villefranche, each a village appellation in its own right, listed here north to south.

places.name: Saint-Amour
places.note: The northernmost cru, across the line in Saône-et-Loire; light, floral and popular on one day in February.

places.name: Juliénas
places.note: Firm, spicy wines on granite and schist with clay to the east; one of the sturdier crus.

places.name: Chénas
places.note: The smallest cru, named for the oaks that once stood there; structured wines close to Moulin-à-Vent in style.

places.name: Moulin-à-Vent
places.note: Named for the windmill above Romanèche-Thorins; manganese-streaked granite gives the deepest, most tannic cru, one that can age ten years and taste like Burgundy.

places.name: Fleurie
places.note: Pink granite and the most perfumed cru: violets, raspberry and silk; the Clos de la Roilette lies on its border with Moulin-à-Vent.

places.name: Chiroubles
places.note: The highest cru, on sandy granite: the lightest and most delicate, drunk young.

places.name: Morgon
places.note: Around Villié-Morgon, one of the largest crus and with Moulin-à-Vent the most ageworthy; cherry and kirsch that turn earthy with age, a change the locals call morgonner.

places.name: Côte du Py
places.note: The hill of decomposed schist above Villié-Morgon, the cru's grandest site and the birthplace of its natural-wine school.

places.name: Régnié
places.note: Promoted in 1988, the most recent of the ten crus as of 2026, on pink granite sand: light, fruity and early drinking.

places.name: Côte de Brouilly

places.name: Brouilly

terroir.climate: Continental, a touch warmer than the Côte d'Or and open to Mediterranean warmth from the south, so Gamay ripens fully; summer hail and spring frost on the lower ground are the hazards, and the Monts du Beaujolais shelter the slopes from western rain.
terroir.soils: Pink granite and schist in the north, weathering to the coarse sand the crus prize; the hard blue stone, the pierre bleue, of Mont Brouilly, manganese-rich granite at Moulin-à-Vent, decomposed schist on the Côte du Py. South of Villefranche the ground turns to clay and the golden limestone of the Pierres Dorées, home of plain Beaujolais.
terroir.topography: Hills rising west of the Saône plain to the forested Monts du Beaujolais, the crus on east and south-east facing slopes between about 200 and 500 metres; Chiroubles is the highest cru and the lightest.
terroir.water: The Saône flows past on the eastern plain and the small Nizerand marks the rough divide between the granite north and the limestone south.

traps: A cru label need not carry the word Beaujolais; Beaujolais-Villages always does.
Nouveau may be Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages, never a cru.
Côte de Brouilly and Brouilly are two crus: the hill and the ring around it.
Beaujolais is in greater Burgundy by law; the grape is Gamay, not Pinot Noir.
Carbonic maceration is a fermentation method, not a grape or a place.
Régnié joined the crus in 1988; there have been ten ever since, not nine or twelve.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the backbone of the Right Bank and of everyday red: early ripening, plummy, soft and fleshy, prone to coulure at flowering.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The Left Bank leader on warm gravel: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, firm tannin and long life, the last grape picked.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Perfume, red fruit and leafy freshness; a large share at Cheval Blanc and across Saint-Émilion, a seasoning in the Médoc.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A late-ripening dash of colour, spice and tannin in Médoc blends, rarely above a tenth.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Historic and now scarce, lingering in Bourg, Blaye and the Côtes; a legal variety that students forget.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.styles: The old Médoc grape nearly lost to phylloxera and still permitted, planted by a few estates as a curiosity.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Thin skinned and botrytis prone, the heart of Sauternes and the weight in dry white, waxy and honeyed with age.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Aroma and acidity for dry white at Entre-Deux-Mers and Pessac-Léognan, and the lift in sweet blends; Sauvignon Gris is its rarer cousin.

grapes.name: Muscadelle
grapes.styles: The third white, grapey and floral, a small seasoning in sweet and dry blends; no relation to Muscat.

law.classification: The appellations run from the regional Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, through the district names such as Médoc, Graves and Entre-Deux-Mers, to the communes: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis-en-Médoc in the Médoc, Pessac-Léognan in the Graves, Sauternes and Barsac for sweet wine, Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac on the Right Bank. Over the appellations sit the estate classifications, each with its own logic. The 1855 list ranked sixty-one red estates, sixty of the Médoc and Haut-Brion, into five growths on price, and ranked Sauternes and Barsac separately under Yquem; it has moved once, when Mouton rose to First Growth in 1973. The Graves classification of 1953, confirmed in 1959, is a single tier of crus classés, all now in Pessac-Léognan, for red, white or both. Saint-Émilion first classified in 1955 and rewrites its list about every ten years; the 2022 edition named Figeac and Pavie Premier Grand Cru Classé A after Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus withdrew. Pomerol has never classified. The Cru Bourgeois du Médoc is a separate five-yearly list below the 1855 growths, last published on 10 February 2025 with 170 estates in three tiers.

Dry white from anywhere in the region; the dry wines of Sauternes estates such as Y of Yquem use it
A Sauternes commune that may label as Barsac or as Sauternes
tiers: Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur
The regional appellations covering the whole vineyard; Supérieur means slightly higher minimum alcohol, lower yields and longer ageing, not a quality rank.
District appellations
Médoc, Haut-Médoc, Graves, Entre-Deux-Mers (dry white and, since 2023, red), Côtes de Bordeaux with its named communes.
Commune appellations
Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc, Moulis-en-Médoc, Pessac-Léognan, Sauternes, Barsac, Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru, Pomerol, Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac.
1855 Classification (Médoc and Sauternes)
Five growths of red, Premier to Cinquième Cru Classé: 5, 14, 14, 10 and 18 estates; Sauternes and Barsac in Premier Cru Supérieur (Yquem alone), Premier Cru and Deuxième Cru.
Graves Cru Classé
The 1953 and 1959 list of sixteen estates, one tier, red and white judged separately; all in Pessac-Léognan.
Saint-Émilion classification
Premier Grand Cru Classé A and B, then Grand Cru Classé, revised about every ten years, most recently in 2022; plain Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation, not a rank.
Cru Bourgeois du Médoc
Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel, Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois, revised every five years; 2020, then 10 February 2025 with 170 estates and 14 Exceptionnel.
Pomerol
No classification of any kind; Pétrus, Le Pin, Trotanoy and Lafleur are unranked.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained low on wires, most often Guyot double, and planted densely in the classed growths, around eight to ten thousand to the hectare on the gravel, so that each vine carries a small crop. The gravel mounds are prized because they drain and warm; a rise of two metres can separate a classed growth from its neighbour. Picking is by hand at the top and by machine across most of the generic appellations, Merlot first and Cabernet Sauvignon last. The hazards are rain at flowering, which causes coulure in Merlot and uneven set, downy mildew through a wet summer, hail, spring frost in the low-lying parts and rot before harvest; the copper and lime spray called Bordeaux mixture was devised here in the 1880s against mildew. Since 2021 the INAO has allowed Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur growers to plant six extra varieties on trial against a warming climate, among them Marselan, Touriga Nacional and Alvarinho, on no more than five per cent of the vineyard and ten per cent of a blend.
made.winemaking: Red grapes are destemmed and fermented in steel, concrete or oak vats with two to four weeks on the skins; malolactic conversion follows, in barrel at ambitious estates. The wine then rests twelve to twenty-four months in the 225-litre barrique, with new oak from a quarter to all of the barrels at the top, racked every few months and traditionally fined with egg white. The assemblage comes in the spring after harvest, when the cellar decides the proportions of each grape and which lots go into the grand vin and which into the second wine. Nearly everything is château bottled, sold through courtiers and négociants on the Place de Bordeaux and offered as futures, en primeur, while still in barrel. Dry whites at Pessac-Léognan are barrel fermented and stirred on their lees; Entre-Deux-Mers whites are often fermented cool in steel; reds have also been permitted since the 2023 vintage. Sauternes is picked in several passes through the vineyard, the tries, taking only the shrivelled botrytised berries, pressed, fermented in barrel and stopped by sulphur or on its own; the finished wine must hold at least 45 grams of sugar per litre and ages for years in oak.

places.name: Left Bank
places.note: The gravel side west of the Gironde and Garonne, Saint-Estèphe down to Sauternes: Cabernet country, the 1855 estates and the whites of the Graves.

places.name: Médoc
places.note: The peninsula north of the city; Haut-Médoc holds the six communes and Médoc AOC the flatter northern land, where Merlot gains as the gravel thins.

places.name: Saint-Estèphe
places.note: The northernmost commune, more clay and sturdier, slower wines: Cos d'Estournel and Montrose are Second Growths, Calon-Ségur a Third, Meyney unclassified.

places.name: Pauillac
places.note: Three First Growths, Lafite, Latour and Mouton, the two Pichons and Lynch-Bages: eighteen classed growths of pure cassis-and-cedar Cabernet.

places.name: Saint-Julien
places.note: No First Growth but five Seconds, the three Léovilles, Ducru-Beaucaillou and Gruaud Larose; the balanced midpoint of claret; Talbot and Beychevelle are Fourths.

places.name: Margaux
places.note: The southern commune of perfume and silk: Château Margaux the First, Palmer and d'Issan Thirds, Rauzan-Ségla and Brane-Cantenac Seconds; twenty-one classed growths, the most of any commune.

places.name: Listrac-Médoc and Moulis-en-Médoc
places.note: Two inland communes with no 1855 growth; Chasse-Spleen at Moulis has long been the model of what a cru bourgeois can be, whatever the current list says.

places.name: Haut-Médoc
places.note: The broad appellation around the communes, with La Lagune and Cantemerle classed in 1855 and Sociando-Mallet unclassified.

places.name: Graves
places.note: The gravel south of the city along the Garonne, the oldest Bordeaux vineyard: red and dry white, with Graves Supérieures and Cérons for sweet wine.

places.name: Pessac-Léognan
places.note: Carved from the northern Graves in 1987, holding Haut-Brion and all sixteen crus classés of 1959: smoky reds and barrel-aged whites from Carbonnieux, Domaine de Chevalier, Haut-Bailly and La Mission Haut-Brion.

places.name: Sauternes and Barsac
places.note: Five communes by the Ciron, Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac, making botrytised sweet wine only; Yquem stands alone as Premier Cru Supérieur.

places.name: Preignac
places.note: Home of Suduiraut, a Premier Cru of 1855, and of Gilette, which ages its wine for decades in concrete.

places.name: Barsac
places.note: Lower and flatter, on limestone, giving lighter and fresher wines: Climens and Coutet are its Premiers Crus; a Barsac may label as Sauternes.

places.name: Right Bank
places.note: The Libournais, on the right bank of the Dordogne around Libourne: Merlot with Cabernet Franc on clay, limestone and small patches of gravel.

places.name: Saint-Émilion
places.note: The limestone town and plateau: côtes estates such as Ausone, Canon, Pavie and Troplong Mondot on the slopes, graves estates Cheval Blanc and Figeac on gravel beside Pomerol; classified in 1955 and about every decade since, last in 2022.

places.name: The satellites
places.note: Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges hyphenate Saint-Émilion to their own names on cooler land to the north.

places.name: Pomerol
places.note: A small plateau of clay and gravel over an iron pan, blue clay under Pétrus at its crown: Le Pin, Trotanoy, Lafleur, L'Église-Clinet, Vieux Château Certan, Clos L'Église and Bellegrave, none classified.

places.name: Lalande-de-Pomerol
places.note: The satellite north across the Barbanne stream, Merlot-led and softer.

places.name: Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac
places.note: Limestone hills west of Libourne, Merlot of grip and value; Canon-Fronsac is the inner slope.

places.name: Castillon and Francs Côtes de Bordeaux
places.note: The clay-limestone hills east of Saint-Émilion, Merlot-led and the best value on the bank.

places.name: Bourg and Blaye
places.note: Across the Gironde from the Médoc: Côtes de Bourg and Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, Merlot with a little surviving Malbec.

places.name: Entre-Deux-Mers
places.note: Hills between the Garonne and Dordogne. Entre-deux-Mers permits dry white and, since 2023, red; other local reds may carry Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur.

places.name: Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont
places.note: Three sweet appellations across the river from Sauternes, botrytised Sémillon at a gentler price.

producers.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
producers.why: Pauillac First Growth, the most elegant of the five, cedar and graphite over power.

producers.name: Château Latour
producers.why: Pauillac First Growth by the estuary, the most powerful and longest-lived; left the en primeur system in 2012.

producers.name: Château Margaux
producers.why: First Growth of its commune, perfume and silk, and a white, Pavillon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

producers.name: Château Haut-Brion
producers.why: The Graves First Growth of 1855, the only one outside the Médoc, with a great dry white.

producers.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
producers.why: Promoted to First Growth in 1973, the one change to the 1855 list; artist labels since 1945.

producers.name: Pétrus
producers.why: Pomerol's blue-clay Merlot, the world's most famous wine from that grape, unclassified.

producers.name: Château Cheval Blanc
producers.why: Cabernet Franc-led Saint-Émilion on gravel beside Pomerol; withdrew from the classification before 2022.

producers.name: Château Ausone
producers.why: The limestone côtes of Saint-Émilion at their finest; also withdrew before 2022.

producers.name: Château Figeac
producers.why: Promoted to Premier Grand Cru Classé A in 2022, unusual for its large Cabernet share.

producers.name: Château Pavie
producers.why: The other Premier Grand Cru Classé A of 2022, on the Saint-Émilion côtes.

producers.name: Château d'Yquem
producers.why: Sauternes, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855 and the world's reference sweet wine.

producers.name: Château Climens
producers.why: Barsac Premier Cru made from Sémillon alone, botrytis with freshness.

producers.name: Château Suduiraut
producers.why: Preignac Premier Cru of classic rich Sauternes.

producers.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
producers.why: Saint-Estèphe Second Growth with the pagoda chai, exotic and long-lived.

producers.name: Château Léoville Las Cases
producers.why: The Saint-Julien Second Growth most often called a First in all but name.

producers.name: Château Palmer
producers.why: Margaux Third Growth that outperforms its rank, Merlot-rich and velvety.

producers.name: Château Lynch-Bages
producers.why: Pauillac Fifth Growth of Second Growth stature, the classic cassis and cigar box.

producers.name: Château Carbonnieux
producers.why: Pessac-Léognan cru classé for both colours, the white a textbook barrel-aged Sauvignon and Sémillon.

producers.name: Le Pin
producers.why: A tiny Pomerol whose Merlot became a cult in the 1980s, proof that the bank needs no classification.

terroir.climate: Maritime and moderate: the Atlantic keeps winters mild and summers warm rather than hot, and the pine forest of the Landes blunts the sea wind and the salt. Rain is the risk at every turn, spoiling flowering in June, bringing mildew through summer and threatening the picking in late September and October. Because no single grape can be relied on, the vineyard is planted to several that flower and ripen at different moments, and the cellar settles the blend each year.
terroir.soils: The Left Bank is deep gravel laid down by ancient rivers in low mounds, the croupes, which drain fast and store the day's warmth, letting late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon finish this far north. The Right Bank is cooler clay over limestone, with a limestone plateau at Saint-Émilion and blue clay at the top of Pomerol, ground that suits Merlot. Sauternes mixes gravel and sand over limestone, and Entre-Deux-Mers is clay and limestone hills.
terroir.topography: Low and open: a wide estuary plain on the Left Bank where a rise of a few metres in gravel decides a vineyard's rank, the hills of Entre-Deux-Mers between the two rivers, and the limestone escarpment and plateau of Saint-Émilion on the Right Bank, the only real slopes in the region.
terroir.water: The Garonne and the Dordogne meet north of the city to form the Gironde, the tidal estuary that moderates the whole region and divides its banks. The small, cold, spring-fed Ciron runs into the warmer Garonne at Barsac, in the Sauternes district, and the autumn mists where they meet breed the noble rot.

traps: Haut-Brion is an 1855 First Growth from Pessac-Léognan in the Graves, not the Médoc.
Pomerol has no classification, so Pétrus holds no rank at all.
Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation; Grand Cru Classé is the classification, and the top of it is Premier Grand Cru Classé A.
Sauternes is sweet by law; the estates' dry wines are sold as Bordeaux Blanc.
Entre-deux-Mers ceased to be white-only with the 2023 vintage: distinguish its appellation wines from other wines grown in the wider geographical area.
Bordeaux Supérieur means more alcohol and ageing, not a higher class of estate.
Merlot, not Cabernet Sauvignon, is the most planted grape of the whole region.
The Cru Bourgeois list changes every five years; an estate on the 2020 list may be off the 2025 one.

wines.note: Cabernet-led: blackcurrant, cedar, pencil shavings and firm tannin, built for a decade or more; decant young bottles and serve at 17 degrees with lamb or beef.
Merlot with Cabernet Franc: plum, truffle and a softer, rounder grip, approachable sooner than the Médoc, for duck, mushrooms and braised dishes.
Merlot at its most plush: velvet tannin, black cherry, chocolate and iron, the smallest great appellation; roast meats and anything with truffle.
Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon fermented and aged in barrel: smoky, waxy, citrus and nut, long lived; for rich fish and lobster.
Dry Sauvignon-led white; an oyster pairing. The appellation also permits reds since 2023.
Botrytised Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc: apricot, honey, saffron and marmalade on bright acidity; serve cool with foie gras, Roquefort or on its own.
The region-wide red with a touch more ripeness and ageing than plain Bordeaux, Merlot-led and medium bodied; the Tuesday-night claret.
Traditional method sparkling, an appellation since 1990, mostly from Sémillon and Sauvignon; little seen outside the region.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Every red of the Côte d'Or and the Côte Chalonnaise: cherry, rose and earth on fine tannin, from supple village wine to grand crus that live for decades.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Steely and unoaked in Chablis, barrel-fermented and nutty on the Côte de Beaune, ripe and rounded in the Mâconnais; also the base of Crémant de Bourgogne.

grapes.name: Aligoté
grapes.styles: Lean, lemony white for Bourgogne Aligoté and the kir; Bouzeron is its one village appellation.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Blended with Pinot Noir in Bourgogne Passe-Tout-Grains and used for Mâcon rouge; its real home is Beaujolais.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Saint-Bris near Auxerre is its single Burgundy appellation.

law.classification: Burgundy ranks ground, not estates. Regional appellations sit at the base; village appellations carry a commune name; premier cru adds a named climat after the village; grand cru stands under the climat name alone, as in Chambertin or Montrachet, and amounts to about one bottle in a hundred. There are thirty-three grand crus: twenty-four on the Côte de Nuits, eight on the Côte de Beaune and the single Chablis Grand Cru with its seven climats. The climats were inscribed by UNESCO in 2015. A wine may always be declassified downward, never promoted.
labels: A named, delimited vineyard parcel; the unit on which the whole hierarchy rests.
A climat in a single owner's hands, such as La Tâche or Clos de Tart.
A domaine bottles its own vineyards; a maison or négociant buys grapes or wine and bottles under its own name.
The charitable hospital founded in 1443, whose wines sell at auction each November.
Old vines; the term is unregulated.
tiers: Régionale

Bourgogne, Bourgogne Aligoté, Bourgogne Passe-Tout-Grains, Coteaux Bourguignons, Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits and de Beaune, Bourgogne Côte d'Or (from the 2017 vintage), Mâcon and Crémant de Bourgogne: about half of all Burgundy.
Village
A commune name on the label, Meursault or Gevrey-Chambertin; a named lieu-dit may follow in smaller type.
Premier Cru
Village plus climat, as in Beaune Premier Cru Clos des Mouches; a blend of several climats is simply village Premier Cru.
Grand Cru
The climat alone, no village name: Chambertin, Musigny, Corton-Charlemagne. Chablis Grand Cru carries its climat after the appellation.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained low on single Guyot or cordon de Royat and planted densely, around ten thousand to the hectare on the Côte d'Or, so each carries a small crop; the permitted yield falls as the tier rises. Spring frost is the first hazard, fought in Chablis with sprinklers that coat the buds in protective ice and with heaters along the rows; hail is the second, and rot in a wet September the third. Picking is by hand on the slopes, and organic and biodynamic farming is widespread. Inheritance split holdings across generations, so a grower may own a few rows in a dozen climats.
made.winemaking: Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir fermented in open vats after a cold soak, the cap punched down, with a choice over whole bunches: stems add spice and grip, destemming gives purer fruit. The wine ages in the 228 litre pièce, the share of new oak rising with the tier, for twelve to eighteen months. Chardonnay is pressed whole and fermented in barrel on the Côte de Beaune, kept on its lees with bâtonnage and taken through malolactic conversion, which softens the acid; lees and barrel give the hazelnut; Chablis more often ferments in steel or old wood to keep its edge. Chaptalisation is allowed within limits in cold years, and above the regional tier a label names the place and the grower, seldom the grape.

places.name: Chablis
places.note: Chardonnay alone on Kimmeridgian marl around the Serein, cold and frost-prone: steely, saline wine that rarely sees new oak, in four tiers.

places.name: Petit Chablis
places.note: The outer plateau on Portlandian limestone: light, sharp and for early drinking.

places.name: Chablis Premier Cru
places.note: Named climats on both banks: Montée de Tonnerre, Fourchaume and Mont de Milieu on the right, Vaillons and Montmains on the left.

places.name: Chablis Grand Cru
places.note: One appellation, seven climats on one south-west facing slope above the town: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir; Les Clos is the most famous.

places.name: Saint-Bris
places.note: Sauvignon Blanc's only Burgundy appellation, since 2003, near Auxerre.

places.name: Irancy
places.note: Pinot Noir red near Auxerre that may carry a little of the local César.

places.name: Côte de Nuits
places.note: The northern half of the Côte d'Or, Marsannay to Corgoloin: almost all Pinot Noir, twenty-four grand crus, and the firmest, longest-lived red Burgundy.

places.name: Marsannay
places.note: The northern gateway, a village appellation since 1987 and the only one with its own rosé.

places.name: Gevrey-Chambertin
places.note: The largest village of the Côte de Nuits and home of nine grand crus, every one carrying the name Chambertin: deep, powerful, earthy Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
places.note: The two great crus at the heart of the slope; Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin, never the reverse.

places.name: The seven other Chambertins
places.note: Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes, each hyphenated to Chambertin; Mazoyères may be sold as Charmes.

places.name: Clos Saint-Jacques
places.note: A premier cru prized and priced as a grand cru.

places.name: Morey-Saint-Denis
places.note: Between Gevrey and Chambolle: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays, the monopole Clos de Tart and a slice of Bonnes-Mares.

places.name: Chambolle-Musigny
places.note: The most perfumed, silkiest reds; grand crus Musigny and Bonnes-Mares, and Les Amoureuses, the premier cru that drinks like one.

places.name: Musigny
places.note: Chambolle's crown and the only grand cru of the Côte de Nuits permitted to make white.

places.name: Vougeot
places.note: Dominated by the walled Clos de Vougeot, enclosed by Cistercian monks and now split among scores of owners, so the grower is everything.

places.name: Flagey-Échezeaux
places.note: Holds the grand crus Échezeaux and Grands Échezeaux; its village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

places.name: Vosne-Romanée
places.note: Six grand crus in one village, Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, La Romanée, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and La Grande Rue: spice, silk and length.

places.name: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche
places.note: Both monopoles of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which has held Romanée-Conti since 1869.

places.name: La Romanée
places.note: The smallest grand cru appellation in France, a monopole just above Romanée-Conti.

places.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
places.note: Firm, earthy, tannic reds with no grand cru; premier crus Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains, Les Pruliers and Les Cailles lie to the south.

places.name: Côte de Beaune
places.note: The southern half of the Côte d'Or, Ladoix to Maranges: the great whites of Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne, Corton as its lone red grand cru, and supple reds capped at premier cru.

places.name: The hill of Corton
places.note: Shared by Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses. Corton, red with a little white, is the Côte d'Or's largest grand cru; Corton-Charlemagne is the white of its upper slopes.

places.name: Savigny-lès-Beaune
places.note: Supple, early-drinking reds and some white, with premier crus such as Les Lavières and Les Vergelesses; Chorey-lès-Beaune on the flat below has none.

places.name: Beaune
places.note: The merchant capital and seat of the Hospices; no grand cru but premier crus Grèves, Clos des Mouches, Clos de la Mousse, Bressandes and Teurons.

places.name: Pommard
places.note: The sturdiest Côte de Beaune red, tannic and iron-edged; Les Rugiens and Les Épenots lead, and Clos des Épeneaux is a monopole.

places.name: Volnay
places.note: Pommard's silky, perfumed neighbour; Clos des Ducs is a monopole, Caillerets and Champans the names to know, Santenots its red grown in Meursault.

places.name: Monthelie, Auxey-Duresses and Saint-Romain
places.note: Side-valley villages behind Volnay and Meursault: lighter, sharper, good value.

places.name: Meursault
places.note: The largest white village: rich, nutty, barrel-fermented Chardonnay with no grand cru; premier crus Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, and high lieux-dits such as Les Tillets.

places.name: Puligny-Montrachet
places.note: The most precise white village: Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet shared with Chassagne, Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet its own; premier crus Les Pucelles and Les Combettes.

places.name: Montrachet
places.note: The most celebrated dry white vineyard in the world, straddling the village boundary.

places.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
places.note: White and red; holds Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet and its shares of Montrachet and Bâtard, with premier crus Morgeot and Caillerets.

places.name: Saint-Aubin
places.note: Up the side valley behind Puligny: taut, mineral white premier crus such as Le Charmois and En Remilly.

places.name: Santenay and Maranges
places.note: The southern end of the slope: honest reds, some white, premier crus but no grand cru.

places.name: Côte Chalonnaise
places.note: South of the Côte d'Or without its unbroken slope: lighter Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, premier crus and no grand cru.

places.name: Bouzeron
places.note: The one village appellation for Aligoté, created in 1997.

places.name: Rully
places.note: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and a centre of Crémant de Bourgogne.

places.name: Mercurey
places.note: The largest Chalonnaise village, mostly firm Pinot Noir with premier crus.

places.name: Givry
places.note: Pinot Noir of charm with a small amount of white.

places.name: Montagny
places.note: Chardonnay only, the southernmost Chalonnaise village, with premier crus.

places.name: Mâconnais
places.note: Burgundy's largest source of Chardonnay: rolling limestone hills north of Beaujolais, warmer and riper, mostly white.

places.name: Mâcon and Mâcon-Villages
places.note: Mâcon-Villages is white only; a commune may hang its name on Mâcon, as at Mâcon-Igé, and the hill villages west of the town are the best.

places.name: Verzé
places.note: Hill village selling white as Mâcon-Verzé, where a great Puligny domaine now farms.

places.name: Milly-Lamartine
places.note: Neighbouring hill village of Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine, farmed by a famous Meursault family.

places.name: Viré-Clessé
places.note: A village appellation since 1999 from two merged communes: ripe Chardonnay, occasionally late-picked.

places.name: Pouilly-Fuissé
places.note: The flagship, under the rocks of Solutré and Vergisson across four villages: barrel-aged Chardonnay, and twenty-two premier cru climats recognised by the INAO on 3 September 2020, from that vintage.

places.name: Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles
places.note: Two small neighbours of Pouilly-Fuissé; Loché may be sold as Vinzelles. Four premier cru climats, one in Loché and three in Vinzelles, were published by the INAO in November 2024 and apply from the 2024 vintage.

places.name: Saint-Véran
places.note: Wraps Pouilly-Fuissé on both sides: fresh Chardonnay, often a good buy.

producers.name: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti
producers.why: The most famous domaine in the world, with the monopoles Romanée-Conti and La Tâche.

producers.name: Domaine Leroy
producers.why: Biodynamic Vosne-Romanée estate whose wines rank with the Romanée-Conti among Burgundy's most sought after.

producers.name: Domaine Armand Rousseau
producers.why: Gevrey-Chambertin's great name: Chambertin, Clos de Bèze and the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques.

terroir.climate: Continental: cold winters, spring frost, summer hail and the chance of rain at harvest, so vintages differ sharply. Chablis is the coldest corner and loses crop to frost in a bad spring; the Mâconnais is warm enough for Chardonnay to ripen fuller and earlier.
terroir.soils: Jurassic limestone and marl throughout. Chablis lies on Kimmeridgian limestone marl full of fossil oysters, with Portlandian limestone on the plateau above for Petit Chablis. The Côte d'Or mixes limestone scree, marl and clay, heavier on the Côte de Nuits, lighter and chalkier around the great white villages.
terroir.topography: The Côte d'Or is a narrow escarpment facing east and south-east; the best vineyards sit mid-slope, above the frost that pools on the flat and below the thin-soiled hilltop. Chablis is rolling hill country on the Serein, and the Mâconnais ends under the limestone rocks of Solutré and Vergisson.
terroir.water: The Serein runs through Chablis and its right bank carries the grand crus. The Saône flows down the plain east of the Côte d'Or, too far off to moderate the slope; drainage rather than water shapes the sites.

traps: Pouilly-Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay; Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc.
Nuits-Saint-Georges, Beaune, Pommard, Volnay and Meursault have no grand cru.
Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune; Musigny the only white of the Côte de Nuits.
Chablis Grand Cru is one appellation with seven climats; Les Clos is a climat, not a village.
A grand cru label carries no village name; a premier cru carries both.
Bourgogne Côte d'Or is a regional appellation, not a village one.
Mâconnais premier crus are Pouilly-Fuissé's, from the 2020 vintage, and since the 2024 vintage four in Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles; none elsewhere as of the 2024 vintage.

wines.note: Steely, saline Chardonnay with green apple and oyster shell, usually unoaked; serve cold with oysters and raw shellfish.
Pinot Noir with cherry, rose, earth and fine tannin; decant the young, pour the mature with duck, lamb or mushrooms.
Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne: barrel-fermented Chardonnay with hazelnut, citrus and stone; serve at 11 to 13 °C with butter sauces and lobster.
Pommard sturdy, Volnay silky, Beaune and Savigny supple; premier cru is the ceiling for all of them.
Riper Chardonnay with peach and honeysuckle, usually unoaked at Mâcon-Villages, often barrel-aged at Pouilly-Fuissé.
Traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Aligoté and Gamay, at least nine months on lees; a crisp aperitif.

exam: Say the traditional method in order: base wine, blending, tirage, second fermentation, lees ageing, riddling, disgorgement, dosage, cork.
Know the dosage ladder in grams per litre, and that Extra Dry sits sweeter than Brut.
Associate Chardonnay with the Côte des Blancs, Pinot Noir with the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar, and Meunier with the western Marne Valley; recognise exceptions.
Hold the ageing minimums: 15 months for non-vintage with 12 on the lees, 36 months for vintage, both counted from tirage.
Know that cru rank attaches to villages: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru.
Match the prestige cuvées to their houses and the label codes NM, RM and CM to what they mean.
Be ready for bottle sizes: magnum 1.5 litres, Jeroboam 3, Methuselah 6, Nebuchadnezzar 15.
Know the three dominant grapes, the eight principal varieties authorised in July 2025, and the separate conditions attached to Voltis.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Especially associated with the Côte des Blancs; often brings freshness, citrus and floral notes. It is the usual grape of Blanc de Blancs, although that term permits other white varieties.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Body, red fruit and structure from the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Bar; Blanc de Noirs and most rosé lean on it.

grapes.name: Meunier
grapes.styles: Later budburst helps Meunier in frost-prone sites. It is particularly important in the western Marne Valley and often adds fruit and roundness; its name alone does not determine how long a wine will age.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: One of the less common principal varieties, alongside Pinot Gris, Arbane, Petit Meslier and Chardonnay rose. Together with Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, these make eight principal varieties under the July 2025 rules. Voltis has separate conditional adaptation status.

law.classification: One appellation, Champagne, covers the whole sparkling vineyard, with Coteaux Champenois for still wine and Rosé des Riceys for one still rosé. Within it the ranking attaches to villages, not vineyards: seventeen communes hold Grand Cru and forty-two hold Premier Cru, a legacy of the échelle des crus, the percentage scale that once set grape prices and no longer fixes any price at all. A label may claim Grand Cru only when every grape came from Grand Cru villages. The producer's status appears as two small letters: NM for a house that buys grapes, RM for a grower who makes wine from its own fruit, CM for a cooperative, RC for a grower selling cooperative-made wine, SR for a family company, ND for a merchant distributor and MA for a buyer's own brand. Sweetness terms are defined by residual sugar, and the ageing minimums run from tirage.

tiers: Champagne AOC
The whole sparkling appellation; the name alone is the guarantee, and the word Champagne is reserved to it in law.
Grand Cru
Seventeen villages rated at the full 100 per cent on the old scale; the label may say Grand Cru only when all the fruit is from them.
Premier Cru
Forty-two villages rated 90 to 99 per cent; the same all-or-nothing rule applies.
Autres crus
The remaining villages, once rated 80 to 89 per cent; most non-vintage blends draw on them.
Coteaux Champenois
Still red, white or rosé from the Champagne vineyard; Bouzy and Aÿ reds are the best known.
Rosé des Riceys
A still rosé of Pinot Noir from the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube, declared only in ripe years.

made.viticulture: Vineyard work includes pruning, shoot positioning, canopy management and monitoring fruit health and ripeness. Chablis, Cordon de Royat, Guyot and Vallée de la Marne are recognised pruning systems; the last is limited to Meunier. Harvest timing varies by commune and grape. Picking is by hand so whole bunches can arrive at the press. Spring frost, hail, rain and disease pressure affect sites and years differently; later-budding Meunier is not immune to damage. Reserve stocks help manage harvest variation. Under the July 2025 specification, Voltis requires an adaptation agreement, normally occupies no more than 5 per cent of the holding and may make up no more than 10 per cent of a blend. Qualifying plantings close to inhabited sites are excluded from the holding-area calculation. Chardonnay rose is a principal variety, not part of that Voltis category.
made.winemaking: Pressing is gentle and fractionated: 4,000 kilograms of grapes yield at most 2,550 litres, the first 2,050 the cuvée and the last 500 the taille. The juice ferments to a dry, sharp still wine, the vin clair, usually in steel, sometimes in oak, and most houses allow malolactic conversion. In spring the winemaker blends across villages, grapes and reserve wines from earlier years for a non-vintage, or from one year alone for a vintage. The blend goes into bottle with the liqueur de tirage, sugar and yeast, and a second fermentation builds about six atmospheres of pressure. The wine then rests on its lees, at least twelve months for non-vintage, while the dead yeast breaks down and gives the bready, biscuit register. Riddling, remuage, walks the sediment into the neck, by hand on pupitres or by machine in gyropalettes; the neck is frozen and the plug expelled at disgorgement; the bottle is topped up with the liqueur d'expédition, whose sugar fixes the sweetness level; then cork, wire cage and label. Fifteen months must pass between tirage and release for non-vintage, thirty-six for vintage.

places.name: Montagne de Reims
places.note: The wooded plateau south of Reims, ringed by villages that face north and east yet rank at the top for Pinot Noir: structure and body for the blend.

places.name: Reims
places.note: The cathedral city, seat of Krug, Roederer, Taittinger, Veuve Clicquot, Ruinart and Pommery, with the crayères beneath it.

places.name: Verzenay
places.note: North-facing Grand Cru with a landmark windmill; firm, long-lived Pinot Noir despite the aspect.

places.name: Verzy
places.note: Grand Cru beside Verzenay, also facing north, Pinot Noir with Chardonnay rising.

places.name: Bouzy
places.note: Grand Cru on the warm southern flank: Pinot Noir for blends and the best-known red Coteaux Champenois.

places.name: Ambonnay
places.note: Grand Cru next to Bouzy, Pinot Noir of depth and the home of celebrated growers.

places.name: Mailly-Champagne, Sillery, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Puisieulx, Louvois
places.note: The Montagne's other five Grand Cru villages; with Verzenay, Verzy, Bouzy and Ambonnay it holds nine of the seventeen.

places.name: Chigny-les-Roses and Rilly-la-Montagne
places.note: Premier Cru villages on the northern slope, Meunier and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Vallée de la Marne
places.note: The river valley west of Épernay includes clay, marl and sandy ground. Meunier is prominent farther west; the eastern valley around Aÿ is strongly associated with Pinot Noir. These are broad tendencies, not exclusive planting rules.

places.name: Épernay
places.note: The trade town on the Marne, home of Moët & Chandon, Pol Roger and Perrier-Jouët and of the Avenue de Champagne.

places.name: Aÿ
places.note: Grand Cru Pinot Noir village on the Grande Vallée, seat of Bollinger and Deutz and the origin of Gosset.

places.name: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ
places.note: Premier Cru next to Aÿ, home of Billecart-Salmon and of Clos des Goisses, a steep walled single vineyard.

places.name: Tours-sur-Marne
places.note: At the eastern end of the Grande Vallée, rated Grand Cru for Pinot Noir; the seat of Laurent-Perrier.

places.name: Hautvillers, Dizy, Cumières and Tauxières
places.note: Premier Cru villages of the Grande Vallée; Hautvillers holds the abbey where Dom Pérignon was cellarer around 1700.

places.name: Pierry
places.note: Premier Cru grower village just south of Épernay, Meunier and Chardonnay.

places.name: Romery
places.note: A small grower village near Hautvillers in the valley's Meunier country.

places.name: Côte des Blancs
places.note: Chalk slopes south of Épernay, strongly associated with Chardonnay and Blanc de Blancs. Exposure and producer decisions still vary; the district name does not guarantee a wine’s lifespan.

places.name: Chouilly
places.note: Northernmost Grand Cru of the Côte, rated 100 for Chardonnay alone.

places.name: Cramant
places.note: Grand Cru on pure chalk, Chardonnay of creamy weight.

places.name: Avize
places.note: Grand Cru at the heart of the Côte, cradle of the grower movement.

places.name: Oger and Oiry
places.note: Grand Cru villages associated with Chardonnay: Oger lies south of Avize towards Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, while Oiry lies to the north-east of Avize.

places.name: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger
places.note: Grand Cru village associated with Chardonnay, including Salon and Krug’s Clos du Mesnil. The individual wine’s style and ageing depend on the producer, cuvée and harvest.

places.name: Vertus
places.note: Premier Cru at the southern end, the Côte's largest village, mostly Chardonnay.

places.name: Côte de Sézanne
places.note: A southern continuation of the Côte des Blancs on the same chalk, Chardonnay that ripens rounder and earlier.

places.name: Côte des Bar
places.note: The Aube's vineyard a hundred kilometres south-east, on Kimmeridgian marl near Chablis: Pinot Noir country, excluded in 1908 and restored in 1927, now a lively grower scene.

places.name: Urville
places.note: Village on the Bar-sur-Aube side, seat of Drappier, a Pinot Noir house.

places.name: Les Riceys
places.note: Three villages in one commune with their own still rosé appellation, Rosé des Riceys.

places.name: Bar-sur-Aube, Bar-sur-Seine and Celles-sur-Ource
places.note: The two towns that name the Côte and a grower village on the Seine side.

places.name: Montgueux
places.note: A lone Chardonnay hill west of Troyes, rich and exotic for the region.

places.name: Massif de Saint-Thierry
places.note: Sandy slopes north-west of Reims, Meunier and Pinot Noir; Merfy is its best-known grower village.

places.name: Vitryat
places.note: A Chardonnay outpost near Vitry-le-François, east of the main districts, on chalk.

producers.name: Bollinger
producers.why: Aÿ house of 1829, Pinot Noir-led and partly fermented in old oak; Special Cuvée NV and La Grande Année vintage.

producers.name: Louis Roederer
producers.why: Reims house of 1776 with unusually large estate vineyards; Cristal, first made for the Russian court in 1876, is its prestige cuvée in clear glass.

producers.name: Moët & Chandon
producers.why: Épernay, 1743, the largest house; Dom Pérignon is its vintage prestige cuvée.

producers.name: Veuve Clicquot
producers.why: Reims, 1772; the widow Clicquot's cellar is credited with riddling in the 1810s; Yellow Label NV is Pinot Noir-led.

producers.name: Pol Roger
producers.why: Épernay family house of 1849; Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is the prestige wine.

producers.name: Taittinger
producers.why: Reims house with a Chardonnay-leaning style; Comtes de Champagne is a Blanc de Blancs prestige cuvée.

producers.name: Billecart-Salmon
producers.why: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ family house of 1818, known for cool fermentation, finesse and a famous rosé.

producers.name: Ruinart
producers.why: The oldest Champagne house, 1729, in Reims; Chardonnay-led, its crayères open to visitors.

producers.name: Salon
producers.why: One wine only: a Blanc de Blancs from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, one vintage, declared a few times a decade.

producers.name: Charles Heidsieck
producers.why: Reims house of 1851 whose non-vintage carries an unusually high share of reserve wine.

producers.name: Piper-Heidsieck
producers.why: Reims house of 1785; a fruit-forward Brut NV, and the prestige cuvée Rare began here before it was given a house name of its own.

producers.name: Laurent-Perrier

producers.name: Larmandier-Bernier
producers.why: Vertus grower, biodynamic Chardonnay with low dosage.

producers.why: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger grower whose Blanc de Blancs set a standard for the village.

producers.name: Philipponnat

terroir.climate: Cool conditions with both oceanic and continental influences help grapes retain acidity. Spring frost, hail and wet-season disease pressure are significant challenges; warm or dry seasons bring different decisions about ripeness and harvest timing. The aim is a balanced base wine rather than deliberately unripe fruit. Voltis is an adaptation variety with disease-resistance benefits and specific controls, not simply a replacement for the established grapes.
terroir.soils: Chalk is important, especially in the Côte des Blancs, Côte de Sézanne and Vitryat: its porosity supports both drainage and water storage. Clay, marl, sand and hard limestone also occur. The Côte des Bar includes Jurassic limestone and marl. Ground varies within every district; a map-level soil description does not establish a parcel’s geology or explain a flavour on its own.
terroir.topography: Low, gentle slopes rather than mountains. The Montagne de Reims is a wooded plateau whose vine-clad flanks face north, east and south; the Côte des Blancs is a single east-facing chalk escarpment south of Épernay; the Marne cuts a valley between them with vines on both banks. The Côte des Bar lies about 100 kilometres south-east, nearer Chablis than Reims.
terroir.water: The Marne runs through the heart of the region, tempering the frost-prone valley slopes and naming the central district; the Aube and the Seine mark the southern vineyards. The sea is far away, felt only as mild, damp westerly air.

traps: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut; Brut Nature is the driest term, not Extra Brut.
Meunier is a major legal grape, and the rules name it plainly, so a server may say Meunier without Pinot.
Rosé by blending red into white is legal in Champagne and almost nowhere else in AOC France.
Grand Cru ranks a whole village, not a vineyard; a Clos on a Champagne label is a walled site, not a rank.
Crémant is traditional-method sparkling wine from elsewhere in France; it may never be called Champagne.
Vintage Champagne needs three years by law, but the great houses hold it far longer; the minimum is not the custom.
The Côte des Bar is in the Aube, not the Marne, and it lies closer to Chablis than to Reims.
A prestige cuvée is a house's own term with no legal definition.

wines.note: The house style and most of what is sold: a blend across grapes, villages and years, dry under 12 grams of sugar, apple, citrus and brioche. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees with oysters, fried food or a whole meal.
From a single harvest year, with release at least 36 months after tirage. The vintage describes the harvest, not a guaranteed level of richness, toastiness or quality.

White-grape Champagne, usually Chardonnay but not necessarily Chardonnay alone. Citrus, floral and developed flavours depend on site, blend and ageing; select a bottle for the dish rather than relying on the category alone.
A white wine from black grapes only, Pinot Noir or Meunier: broader, red-fruited and vinous, for roast chicken or duck.
Usually made by adding a little still red to the blend, legal here and almost nowhere else in France, sometimes by saignée; dry berry fruit for salmon and lamb.
A house's top bottling, often vintage and long aged: Dom Pérignon, Cristal, Comtes de Champagne, Grande Cuvée. The term has no legal definition.
32 to 50 grams of sugar: gently sweet, for fruit desserts, wedding cake and pastry.
Still wine from the Champagne vineyard in all three colours; the light red of Bouzy or Aÿ is the one a list carries.
A still Pinot Noir rosé from one Aube commune, made only in ripe years, deeper than most pink wine.

exam: Know the three tiers, Vin de France, IGP and AOC, and the 1935 law behind the AOC.
Say what cru means in each region: estate in Bordeaux, vineyard in Burgundy and Alsace, village in Champagne, an appellation of its own in Beaujolais and the Rhône.
Match grape to region for the classics: many appellation labels emphasise place. Alsace is known for varietal labelling, but it is not the only French region to name grapes.
Hold the sweetness words, still and sparkling, and know that Extra Dry sits sweeter than Brut.
Know the eight Crémants, the Vins Doux Naturels and Vin Jaune as the country's other methods.
Expect the Loire, Rhône and Burgundy ladders from regional name to village to cru.

france.overview:
Vines came with the Greeks to Marseille in the sixth century BC and spread with Rome up the Rhône, the Garonne and the Loire. The Church held the great vineyards of Burgundy and Champagne through the Middle Ages, and the Revolution broke them into the small holdings that make Burgundy so complicated today. Phylloxera arrived in the 1860s and forced the whole country onto American rootstocks. The map runs from the Atlantic west, Bordeaux, the Loire mouth and Cognac, through the continental north-east of Champagne, Alsace, Burgundy and Beaujolais, to the Mediterranean south of the Rhône, Provence and Languedoc-Roussillon, with Jura and Savoie against the Alps, the South West behind Bordeaux and Corsica offshore.

The appellation system grew out of the fraud and overproduction that followed phylloxera. Châteauneuf-du-Pape wrote the first modern rules for itself in 1923, the national appellation committee, today’s INAO, was founded by the decree-law of 1935 and the AOC decrees followed. Under the EU scheme of 2009 the AOC is also an AOP, Vin de Pays became IGP and Vin de Table became Vin de France. Each AOC fixes the area, the grapes, the yields, the minimum ripeness and the methods. Above that floor every region ranks differently: Bordeaux ranks estates in the growths of 1855, Burgundy and Alsace rank vineyards, Champagne ranks villages, Beaujolais and the Rhône name their crus as separate appellations, and Saint-Émilion rewrites its list about every ten years. Many French appellations emphasise place rather than grape. Alsace is particularly associated with varietal labelling, but IGP, Vin de France and other permitted appellation labels can also name grapes.

The exam leans on grape-to-place matching, on the meaning of cru, on Champagne's dosage ladder and method, Burgundy's four-tier pyramid, the 1855 First Growths, the northern and southern Rhône, the Loire's four districts and Alsace's noble grapes and two late-harvest categories. It expects the label words: mis en bouteille au château or au domaine, négociant, vieilles vignes, supérieur, sec and demi-sec, brut and extra dry. It also expects the other methods France gave the world: the eight Crémant appellations, Vin Doux Naturel by mutage, Vin de Liqueur, and the Jura's Vin Jaune under its veil of yeast.

law.classification: The base is Vin de France, then the IGPs: Pays d'Oc for the whole region and the departmental ones, Hérault, Aude, Gard and Côtes Catalanes among them. AOC Languedoc, renamed from Coteaux du Languedoc in 2007, is the regional appellation from Nîmes to the Spanish border and may carry a named sub-zone such as Pézenas. Above it the crus hold their own appellations: Faugères and Saint-Chinian (1982), Minervois and Corbières (1985), Fitou (1948), Picpoul de Pinet (2013), Terrasses du Larzac (2014), La Clape (2015), Pic Saint-Loup (2017), and the two village crus, Minervois-La Livinière (1999) and Corbières-Boutenac (2005), both now under their own names, La Livinière and Boutenac, approved by the European Union in March 2024; Montpeyroux, inside the Terrasses du Larzac, was approved by the INAO in June 2025 as a red-only appellation, from the 2026 vintage. Roussillon climbs from Côtes du Roussillon to Côtes du Roussillon Villages with five named communes, with Collioure for dry wine, and Banyuls, Banyuls Grand Cru, Maury and Rivesaltes for the fortified wines.

made.viticulture: Two vineyards share the arc. On the plain, vines are wire trained, machine pruned and machine picked, irrigation is allowed under the IGP rules in dry years, and yields run high for varietal wine. In the hills the old way survives: Carignan and Grenache as bush vines, en gobelet, low against the tramontane and the mistral, many of them over fifty years old, with Syrah and Mourvèdre on wires beside them; the appellations fix low yields and require blends of at least two principal grapes. The dry wind keeps mildew and rot rare, which has made this one of France's largest organic vineyards, and the hazards are drought, water stress, heat spikes at véraison, hail and summer fire in the garrigue. Harvest starts in August for the Muscats and the sparkling base and runs into October for Mourvèdre and Carignan. Vine-pull schemes since the 1980s took out much of the bulk vineyard, and the coteaux were replanted to the Rhône grapes.
made.winemaking: The hill reds are destemmed or part whole bunch and fermented in concrete, steel or large wood; Carignan is often given carbonic maceration to tame its tannin and bring out fruit, and the finished blend is aged in old foudre or barrique. Cooperatives still make much of the volume, and the IGP wines are made cold and clean in steel for export. Picpoul is made cold in steel, Limoux's Chardonnay in barrel. Blanquette and Crémant de Limoux go through the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle; the méthode ancestrale bottles Mauzac before its first fermentation is finished, so it finishes sweet and low in alcohol. The vins doux naturels are made by mutage: during fermentation, when the must is still rich in sugar, five to ten per cent of neutral grape spirit at 96 per cent is added and the yeast stops, leaving sweetness and 15 to 18 per cent alcohol; the must needs at least 252 grams of sugar per litre. Grenat and rimage are bottled young; ambré, tuilé, rancio and hors d'âge age for years in old casks and glass bonbonnes left out in the sun.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean throughout: hot, dry summers, mild winters and generous sun, with rain in autumn and spring storms and long droughts between. The winds matter: the tramontane in Roussillon and the western Languedoc and the mistral in the east blow dry and cold, cutting rot and disease so that organic farming is easy, but stressing the vines. The Atlantic reaches the far west around Carcassonne and Limoux, cooling Cabardès and the sparkling vineyards.
terroir.soils: A mosaic. Schist runs through Faugères, the northern half of Saint-Chinian, the Agly valley of Roussillon and the terraces of Banyuls, where its dark surface holds heat for Grenache. Limestone and clay-limestone carry La Clape, Pic Saint-Loup and the southern half of Saint-Chinian; Terrasses du Larzac mixes limestone scree with rounded stones; Minervois and Corbières hold both, with sandstone and marl; the coastal plain is deep alluvium.
terroir.topography: A crescent of plain along the coast rising into the foothills of the Massif Central, the Larzac causse and the Cévennes, the Montagne Noire above the Minervois, the rugged Corbières massif and the Pyrenees over Roussillon, where terraced vineyards drop straight into the sea at Banyuls. Quality follows altitude and slope: coteaux over plain.
terroir.water: The Mediterranean and the lagoons behind it, the Bassin de Thau among them, where Picpoul de Pinet faces the oyster beds of Bouzigues. The Aude, Hérault and Orb flow out of the hills; in Roussillon the Agly, Têt and Tech valleys sort the vineyards.

traps: Fitou lies inside Corbières country and predates it as an appellation: 1948 against 1985.
Picpoul de Pinet is a white from Piquepoul; Pinet is the village, not a grape.
Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes are fortified sweet wines; Collioure and Maury Sec are the dry wines of the same ground.
Muscat de Rivesaltes may use Muscat of Alexandria; the four Languedoc Muscats use Muscat à Petits Grains alone.
Blanquette de Limoux is Mauzac-based and the Crémant is Chardonnay and Chenin-led; both are traditional method, only the méthode ancestrale is not.
Pic Saint-Loup makes no white under its own name; La Clape does.
Terrasses du Larzac is red only; Faugères and Saint-Chinian make all three colours.
Vin doux naturel is not naturally sweet wine in the Sauternes sense: the sugar is kept by adding spirit.

The dry wine of the Banyuls terraces: Grenache and Mourvèdre reds of sun and salt, rosé and white; a grower chooses yearly between Collioure and Banyuls.
Grenache vin doux naturel from the sea terraces: young and reductive as rimage, or aged in old wood and glass bonbonnes to rancio; the chocolate wine.
Grenache vin doux naturel from the black schist of the upper Agly, deeper and more tannic than Banyuls; dry red Maury Sec since 2011.

France's largest IGP: varietal wines from the plain, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Viognier, clean and ripe, priced for the glass.

law.classification: The Loire follows the national ladder of Vin de France, IGP and AOC, with IGP Val de Loire (once Jardin de la France) covering the valley's country wine. The appellations are named for places and the grape is implied: Muscadet is Melon, Vouvray is Chenin, Sancerre white is Sauvignon, Chinon is Cabernet Franc. Rank above the village level is rare. Quarts de Chaume became the valley's first and only Grand Cru in 2011 and Chaume its only Premier Cru, within Coteaux du Layon; Savennières carries two named crus, Coulée de Serrant and Roche aux Moines; and Muscadet Sèvre et Maine had seven crus communaux in its rules by early 2026, the first three recognised in 2011, with longer lees ageing; La Haie-Fouassière, Vallet and Champtoceaux (in the Coteaux de la Loire) were put to public consultation in 2025. Sweetness words (sec, demi-sec, moelleux, doux) and sur lie are regulated terms, not house style. Crémant de Loire is the valley-wide traditional-method appellation.

Seven named villages in Sèvre et Maine by early 2026, Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet first in 2011, with lower yields and at least a year and a half to two years on the lees; La Haie-Fouassière, Vallet and Champtoceaux in the Coteaux de la Loire were proposed in 2025.
Premier Cru and Grand Cru
Chaume (Premier Cru, in Coteaux du Layon) and Quarts de Chaume (Grand Cru, 2011) are the valley's only ranked tiers.

made.viticulture: Each district trains and picks to its own grape. Melon around Nantes grows on low Guyot vines over granite and gneiss, picked early to keep acidity high and alcohol low, with April frost off the Atlantic as the great hazard. Chenin is picked in several passes, tries, in Anjou and at Vouvray: a first for dry wine, later ones as the berries shrivel or take noble rot, so one slope can give sec, demi-sec and moelleux in a single autumn, and the grower decides only once the weather has shown its hand. Cryoextraction and chaptalisation are barred at Quarts de Chaume. Cabernet Franc in Touraine ripens on warm gravels and tuffeau slopes but must be picked fully ripe to avoid green pepper. Sauvignon in the Centre is wire-trained, machine-picked on flatter land and hand-picked on the steep Monts Damnés. Organic and biodynamic farming are widespread at Vouvray, Savennières, Montlouis and Sancerre.
made.winemaking: Muscadet's signature is sur lie: the wine stays on its fine lees through the winter without racking and is bottled straight off them from the March after harvest, taking a faint prickle of carbon dioxide and a yeasty roundness; the crus communaux go further, with around two years on the lees. Chenin ferments slowly, often in old demi-muids or neutral barrels, sometimes in steel; sweet wines stop on their own or by chilling and sulphur with the sugar they keep, and in the tuffeau caves they age for decades. Crémant de Loire and Vouvray mousseux and pétillant are traditional-method sparkling wines with a second fermentation in bottle; Montlouis's Pétillant Originel is bottled before the first fermentation ends, with no dosage. Cabernet Franc is destemmed, fermented at moderate temperatures and aged in old wood or concrete to keep its fruit. Sauvignon in the Centre is mostly steel and bottled early, though Chavignol's best sites see older oak, and the reds are light Pinot Noir with little new wood.

places.name: Pays Nantais
places.note: Around Nantes at the Atlantic mouth: Melon de Bourgogne on granite, gneiss, schist and gabbro, dry and saline, sur lie its signature.

places.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
places.note: The largest and best Muscadet appellation, south-east of Nantes between its two rivers; home of sur lie and the crus communaux.

places.name: Crus communaux
places.note: Clisson, Gorges, Le Pallet, Goulaine, Château-Thébaud, Monnières-Saint-Fiacre and Mouzillon-Tillières, the seven in the rules by early 2026: village wines held around two years on their lees. La Haie-Fouassière, Vallet and Champtoceaux were put to consultation in 2025.

places.name: Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu and Coteaux de la Loire
places.note: The two smaller Muscadet zones, by the lake south-west of Nantes and upstream towards Ancenis.

places.name: Gros Plant du Pays Nantais
places.note: Sharp, light white from Folle Blanche, the region's other grape.

places.name: Anjou-Saumur
places.note: Chenin Blanc on schist and then tuffeau around Angers and Saumur: dry Savennières, sweet Layon, the valley's rosés, Cabernet Franc at Saumur-Champigny and Saumur's sparkling cellars.

places.name: Savennières
places.note: Dry Chenin on dark schist on the north bank near Angers; two named crus inside it, Coulée de Serrant (a monopole) and Roche aux Moines.

places.name: Coteaux du Layon
places.note: Botrytised Chenin on the Layon's slopes, village names allowed on the label, Chaume as Premier Cru.

places.name: Quarts de Chaume
places.note: The Loire's only Grand Cru since 2011, a sheltered slope above Chaume; no chaptalisation, no cryoextraction.

places.name: Bonnezeaux
places.note: A second sweet Chenin appellation inside the Layon zone, on schist slopes.

places.name: Coteaux de l'Aubance
places.note: Sweet Chenin from the next valley north of the Layon, lighter in style.

places.name: Rochefort-sur-Loire
places.note: The village between Savennières and the Layon, with cellars making dry, sweet and Quarts de Chaume alike.

places.name: Anjou, Anjou-Villages, Rosé d'Anjou, Cabernet d'Anjou
places.note: The regional names: Chenin whites, Cabernet reds and off-dry pinks; Anjou-Villages Brissac is the stricter red.

places.name: Saumur
places.note: The town and regional appellation: Chenin whites, Cabernet reds, and tuffeau caves that age Crémant de Loire and Saumur mousseux.

places.name: Saumur-Champigny
places.note: Cabernet Franc on tuffeau south-east of Saumur, the valley's most polished red.

places.name: Saumur Puy-Notre-Dame and Coteaux de Saumur
places.note: A newer village red appellation and the sweet Chenin of the Saumur side.

places.name: Touraine
places.note: The middle Loire around Tours: Chenin at Vouvray and Montlouis, Cabernet Franc at Chinon and Bourgueil, Sauvignon and Gamay under the Touraine name.

places.name: Vouvray
places.note: Chenin on the north bank east of Tours, on tuffeau: sec, demi-sec, moelleux, mousseux and pétillant from the same slopes.

places.name: Montlouis-sur-Loire
places.note: Vouvray's mirror on the south bank, Chenin alone, with Pétillant Originel.

places.name: Chinon
places.note: Cabernet Franc on the Vienne, gravel for early drinking and tuffeau slopes for ageing, plus a little Chenin white.

places.name: Bourgueil
places.note: Cabernet Franc on the north bank, firmer and longer-lived than Chinon.

places.name: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
places.note: The lighter, sandier neighbour of Bourgueil, Cabernet Franc for early drinking.

places.name: Touraine AOC
places.note: Sauvignon Blanc white and Gamay red across the district, with communal names such as Chenonceaux.

places.name: Cheverny and Cour-Cheverny

places.name: Jasnières and Coteaux du Loir

places.name: Valençay
places.note: Red, white and rosé at Touraine's eastern edge, sharing its name with a goat cheese.

places.name: Centre

places.name: Sancerre
places.note: The hill town on the left bank: Sauvignon on caillottes, terres blanches and silex; red and rosé from Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chavignol
places.note: The Sancerre village with the steep Monts Damnés on Kimmeridgian marl, and the Crottin goat cheese.

places.name: Pouilly-Fumé
places.note: Sauvignon on the right bank around Saint-Andelain, flint-smoked, white only.

places.name: Pouilly-sur-Loire
places.note: The same ground as Pouilly-Fumé, planted to Chasselas, plain and local.

places.name: Menetou-Salon
places.note: Sancerre's neighbour on the same Kimmeridgian marl: Sauvignon and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Quincy and Reuilly

places.name: Coteaux du Giennois and Châteaumeillant
places.note: Outer Centre appellations: Sauvignon and light reds near Gien, Gamay vin gris to the south.

places.name: Orléans and Orléans-Cléry
places.note: Small appellations around Orléans, the latter for Cabernet Franc red.

places.name: Crémant de Loire
places.note: The valley-wide traditional-method sparkling appellation across Anjou, Saumur and Touraine, Chenin-led, centred on Saumur.

places.name: Val de Loire
places.note: IGP Val de Loire, the whole valley's country wine: varietal Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Gamay, grape on the label.

places.name: Upstream and outlying appellations
