terroir.climate: Maritime at Nantes, mild and damp with Atlantic frost in spring; increasingly continental upstream, so Sancerre has hard winters, hot summers and a real frost risk each April. Rain at harvest and rot are the autumn hazards, except on the Layon, where sheltering hills bring the misty mornings and dry afternoons that noble rot needs.
terroir.soils: Two basements meet near Saumur. To the west lies the old, hard Armorican rock, granite, gneiss, schist and gabbro, which gives Muscadet its salt and Savennières its austerity; to the east begins the soft Cretaceous limestone of the Paris Basin, the tuffeau, quarried for châteaux and cellars. The Centre adds Kimmeridgian marl (terres blanches), hard pebbly limestone (caillottes) and flint (silex), whose Sauvignon smells of struck match and gunsmoke.
terroir.topography: A broad, low valley with vines on gentle slopes and terraces above the floodplain, rarely higher than 300 metres. Tributaries carry the best sites: the Sèvre and Maine around Nantes, the Layon and Aubance in Anjou, the Cher, Indre and Vienne in Touraine. Sancerre is a steep hill town above the river, Pouilly its lower-lying neighbour on the opposite bank.
terroir.water: The Loire runs about 1,000 kilometres from the Massif Central to the Atlantic, and every district faces it or a tributary. The Sèvre and Maine name the best Muscadet; the Layon's mists make the sweet wines; the Cher, Indre, Vienne and Loir carry Touraine's appellations; Sancerre sits on the left bank, Pouilly-Fumé on the right.

traps: Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon; Pouilly-Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay; Pouilly-sur-Loire is Chasselas from Pouilly-Fumé's own ground.
Muscadet's grape is Melon de Bourgogne, not Muscat and not a grape called Muscadet.
Sancerre rouge is Pinot Noir, never Cabernet Franc.
Savennières is dry Chenin by custom and nearly always in the bottle; the sweet Layon wines are the same grape with the opposite intent.
Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou are off-dry; Rosé de Loire is the dry one.
A Vouvray is not dry by default: read the label for sec, demi-sec or moelleux.
Fumé Blanc is a California name borrowed from Pouilly-Fumé, not a Loire appellation.
Chenin Blanc is also Steen in South Africa; the Loire never calls it that.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: The body and the strawberry fruit of most rosé and of the reds of Aix, Les Baux and the Var; bush trained and drought hardy.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: The rosé grape above all: pale, soft, low in tannin, bringing delicacy and a redcurrant lift to the blend.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Colour, pepper and structure in reds and a share of the rosé blends, strongest in the cooler inland Var.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Bandol's grape, at least half of every red there: dark, meaty, tannic and slow, with the sea's warmth needed to ripen it.

grapes.name: Tibouren
grapes.styles: Provence's own rosé speciality, the same vine as Liguria's Rossese and scarcely grown elsewhere in France: delicate, herbal and pale, prized on the coast around Saint-Tropez.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Called Rolle here; the main white grape, dry, citrus and fennel, and a small lifting share of many rosés.

grapes.name: Clairette
grapes.styles: A traditional white of Cassis, Palette and the hills: low in acid, floral and full.

grapes.name: Marsanne
grapes.styles: Leads the white of Cassis with Clairette and Ugni Blanc, giving weight and a honeyed edge.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Permitted in Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence and Les Baux-de-Provence as a blending partner for Syrah and Grenache; Trévallon's half-Cabernet red left the appellation for the IGP over its share.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Old vines survive in the Var; capped in most appellation blends and fading.

grapes.name: Braquet
grapes.styles: A Bellet grape for perfumed rosé and light red, with Folle Noire for the deeper reds of that one hillside.

law.classification: Nine appellations and a wide IGP net. Côtes de Provence, created in 1977, is by far the largest, running across the Var into the Bouches-du-Rhône and a corner of the Alpes-Maritimes, and carries five named sub-zones that may follow its name on the label: Sainte-Victoire and Fréjus from 2005, La Londe from 2008, Pierrefeu from 2013 and Notre-Dame des Anges from 2019. Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence (1985) covers the west and Coteaux Varois en Provence (1993) the centre. The small historic appellations are Cassis (1936), Bandol and Bellet (1941), Palette (1948), Les Baux-de-Provence (1995) and Pierrevert (1998). Inside Côtes de Provence a classification of 1955 named twenty-three estates Cru Classé; the title belongs to the land, cannot be won anew and is still used by most of them. Below the appellations sit IGP Méditerranée, IGP Var, IGP Bouches-du-Rhône and IGP Alpilles, where growers such as Trévallon work outside the appellation grape rules.

made.viticulture: Grenache and Mourvèdre were traditionally bush vines, en gobelet, low to the ground against the mistral, and old vines stay that way; most of the rosé vineyard is now trained on wires in cordon de Royat or Guyot so that machines can pick fast at night and bring cool fruit to the press. Picking for rosé comes early, before the sugars climb, since the style wants moderate alcohol and acidity. The dry air keeps mildew and rot down, which is why organic farming is so widespread here. The hazards are drought and water stress in the hot years, with irrigation tightly limited, the mistral snapping young shoots in the west, late spring frost in the inland valleys and summer fire in the pine and scrub. At Bandol the vines stand on stone-walled terraces in a south-facing amphitheatre, picked by hand, and Mourvèdre is planted where the sea's heat reaches it, because it ripens later than anything around it; the rules require at least half of a red to be Mourvèdre, and most growers go well above that.
made.winemaking: Rosé is the craft. The two routes are direct pressing of whole grapes, which gives the palest wine, and a few hours of skin contact before the juice is drawn off, the saignée; either way the point is to take colour and little tannin. The juice is settled cold, fermented cool in stainless steel, usually kept from malolactic conversion to hold the freshness, sometimes left on fine lees for texture, and bottled within months, since the wine is meant for the coming summer. Blending is the rule: Côtes de Provence rosé must combine grapes, never one alone, and Rolle may add a white lift. The Centre du Rosé at Vidauban, founded in 1999, is the research station that set the colour scale and the modern style. The reds of Bandol are the opposite temper: Mourvèdre, Grenache and Cinsault go through long maceration and then at least eighteen months in wood, traditionally large old foudres, before sale, emerging tannic and reductive and built for a decade. Cassis and Palette whites are fermented dry and often rested in old wood; at Palette, Château Simone rests its wines in old wood for years.

places.name: Côtes de Provence
places.note: The great rosé appellation from the Var coast to the hills behind Saint-Tropez and the slopes of Sainte-Victoire, with Minuty at Gassin and Esclans at La Motte-en-Provence among its best-known estates.

places.name: Sainte-Victoire
places.note: Limestone slopes under the mountain painted by Cézanne, east of Aix; a sub-zone since 2005 for red and rosé.

places.name: Fréjus
places.note: Volcanic and crystalline soils of the Esterel on the eastern coast; a sub-zone since 2005, Tibouren at home here.

places.name: La Londe
places.note: Schist by the sea near Hyères, a sub-zone since 2008 and the only one of the five with a white beside its mineral rosé and red.

places.name: Pierrefeu and Notre-Dame des Anges
places.note: The two inland sub-zones of the central Var, added in 2013 and 2019, the second the most recent of the five as of 2026.

places.name: Vidauban
places.note: The village in the Var holding the Centre du Rosé, the research station that defined the pale modern style.

places.name: Bandol
places.note: A south-facing amphitheatre of terraces around the fishing port west of Toulon, across La Cadière-d'Azur, Le Castellet, Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer and their neighbours: Mourvèdre reds of real age, a serious rosé and a little white.

places.name: Le Plan du Castellet
places.note: The hamlet below Le Castellet where Domaine Tempier set the standard for Mourvèdre after the appellation came in 1941.

places.name: La Cadière-d'Azur
places.note: The hilltop village whose high limestone terraces hold Pibarnon and some of the appellation's coolest sites.

places.name: Cassis
places.note: The small calanque port east of Marseille, an appellation of 1936 and the region's white-wine name: Marsanne, Clairette and Ugni Blanc on limestone above the sea.

places.name: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence
places.note: The western appellation around Aix and the Durance, limestone and the mistral, red and rosé with Cabernet Sauvignon allowed beside Grenache and Syrah.

places.name: Les Baux-de-Provence and the Alpilles
places.note: The jagged limestone ridge north of Arles: an appellation since 1995, almost wholly organic, red and rosé with white admitted in 2011, and the IGP Alpilles beside it, where Domaine de Trévallon makes its Cabernet and Syrah red and a Marsanne-led white at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès.

places.name: Palette
places.note: A few hillsides at Meyreuil just east of Aix, an appellation since 1948 dominated by Château Simone: oak-aged red, white and rosé from a long roll of old varieties.

places.name: Bellet
places.note: Terraces in the hills behind Nice on pebbly conglomerate, an appellation since 1941: Braquet and Folle Noire for rosé and red, Rolle for white.

places.name: Coteaux Varois en Provence
places.note: The centre of the Var around Brignoles, higher and cooler than the coast, an appellation since 1993; the rosés are a touch firmer.

places.name: Pierrevert
places.note: The highest Provence appellation, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence near Manosque, since 1998; fresher wines in all three colours.

producers.name: Domaine Tempier
producers.why: The reference for Bandol red and rosé, the estate that built the appellation's name on Mourvèdre.

producers.name: Château de Pibarnon
producers.why: High limestone terraces at La Cadière-d'Azur giving the most elegant, long-lived Bandol.

producers.name: Château Pradeaux
producers.why: Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer traditionalist whose Bandol reds are near pure Mourvèdre and need a decade.

producers.name: Domaines Ott
producers.why: The house that made Provence rosé a luxury, with crus classés at Château de Selle and Clos Mireille and a Bandol estate.

producers.name: Château Minuty
producers.why: Cru Classé at Gassin on the Saint-Tropez peninsula; its pale rosés are on lists worldwide.

producers.name: Château d'Esclans
producers.why: La Motte-en-Provence estate behind Whispering Angel and the oak-fermented Garrus, the wines that priced rosé upward.

producers.name: Château Simone
producers.why: Nearly the whole of Palette: foudre-aged white, red and rosé from very old vines.

producers.name: Domaine de Trévallon
producers.why: The Alpilles estate whose Cabernet and Syrah red is bottled as IGP because the appellation caps Cabernet.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean: long hot summers, mild winters and close to three thousand hours of sunshine a year, with rain falling mostly in spring and autumn storms. The mistral blows cold and dry down the Rhône corridor across the western half, cooling the vines and keeping rot away but breaking shoots. Nearer the coast sea breezes temper the heat, and inland the Var hills climb into cooler nights. Drought, water stress and forest fire are the modern hazards.
terroir.soils: The west, from the Alpilles through Aix, Sainte-Victoire, Cassis and Bandol, is limestone and clay-limestone country, often as bare white rock and scree. East of a line near Toulon the old crystalline massifs take over: the Maures and the Esterel bring schist, gneiss, granite and red porphyry, giving the darker, more mineral rosés of the coast. Bandol's terraces mix limestone with sandstone and marl, and Bellet sits on a pebbly conglomerate above Nice.
terroir.topography: An arc of hills and short mountain ridges between the Rhône delta and the Italian border: the Alpilles, the Sainte-Victoire and Sainte-Baume ridges, the Maures along the coast and the Esterel at Fréjus. The vineyards sit in valleys and on terraced slopes, the restanques, and in the natural amphitheatres that open to the sea at Bandol and Cassis. Pierrevert, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, is the highest and coolest.
terroir.water: The Mediterranean runs the whole southern edge and moderates the coast; the Rhône marks the west and the Durance crosses the north. Bandol's bay faces due south, which is what lets Mourvèdre ripen.

traps: Cassis the appellation is dry white wine from a port near Marseille; crème de cassis is the blackcurrant liqueur of Burgundy.
Bandol makes a fine rosé, but the exam's Bandol answer is Mourvèdre red.
Cru Classé in Provence is a 1955 list of estates inside Côtes de Provence, nothing to do with 1855.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The sole black grape of the north: black pepper, violet, olive and smoked meat on firm tannin, from Côte-Rôtie's perfume to Cornas's rugged depth; a blending partner for colour and spice in the south.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: The backbone of the south: raspberry, kirsch, garrigue and warmth, bush-trained in Châteauneuf, Gigondas and Côtes du Rhône, and fortified as Rasteau.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Late-ripening and tannic, adding meat, structure and keeping power to southern blends; a lead at some Châteauneuf estates.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot, honeysuckle and oily weight at Condrieu and Château-Grillet; up to a fifth co-fermented into Côte-Rôtie.

grapes.name: Marsanne
grapes.styles: The northern white workhorse: honeysuckle, quince and waxy weight in Hermitage Blanc, Saint-Joseph, Crozes and Saint-Péray.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: Marsanne's aromatic partner, finer and harder to grow; a white Châteauneuf grape too.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Soft red fruit and freshness in southern blends; a mainstay of Tavel rosé.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: An accessory grape in Côtes du Rhône blends, capped by the rules.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: The grape of the fortified Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and the sweet sparkling Clairette de Die.

grapes.name: Counoise
grapes.styles: A peppery Châteauneuf variety, prized by a few estates for spice and acidity.

grapes.name: Clairette
grapes.styles: A southern white with soft acid, the lead of Gigondas white and a partner in white Châteauneuf.

law.classification: The valley carries one ladder. Côtes du Rhône, the base, covers both zones though nearly all of it is southern; Côtes du Rhône Villages demands lower yields and a higher share of Grenache; a Villages wine from a listed commune may add that name, Séguret or Sablet; and the crus, eight in the north and, with Laudun, ten in the south, stand under their own names with no mention of the Rhône. Two vins doux naturels and the Diois sparkling appellations sit alongside, with Ventoux, Luberon, Costières de Nîmes and Grignan-les-Adhémar as the satellites. The crus have grown: Vinsobres in 2006, Rasteau for dry wine in 2010, Cairanne from the 2015 vintage, and Laudun, approved by the INAO on 11 September 2024 for red and white from that vintage.
labels: Sweet wine fortified during fermentation; Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau.

A tighter zone with lower yields; red at least half Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre at least a fifth.
Villages with a named commune

Cru

made.viticulture: Northern vines grow on terraces so steep that almost all work is by hand, and Syrah is trained on single wooden stakes, échalas, or on two crossed poles against the mistral; the walls need endless repair. Yields are low and harvest, from September, is by hand. In the south Grenache is grown as a low gobelet bush, pruned short so it withstands wind and drought, with Syrah on wires; Châteauneuf-du-Pape requires hand harvest and sorting of the crop, and sets its minimum alcohol at 12.5 per cent with no chaptalisation. The mistral dries the canopy and keeps fungal disease rare, which is why organic farming is so widespread in the south, but it also shreds shoots and can cut the crop. The galets of La Crau store the day's heat and release it at night, and sand such as that under Rayas gives a lighter, more perfumed Grenache. White vines were long interplanted among the black in the north and picked together, which is the root of the co-fermentation rules.
made.winemaking: Northern Syrah is often fermented with a share of whole bunches, the stems adding pepper and structure, and the permitted white grapes go into the vat with the black and ferment there, never blended in afterwards: up to twenty per cent Viognier at Côte-Rôtie, fifteen per cent Marsanne and Roussanne at Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage, ten per cent at Saint-Joseph, none at Cornas. Ageing is in larger old barrels or demi-muids, with new oak a house choice rather than a rule. Southern reds are blends assembled after fermentation, Grenache usually raised in concrete or large foudres because it oxidises easily in small new wood, Syrah and Mourvèdre sometimes in barrel. The whites are mostly unoaked and drunk young, Hermitage Blanc the exception. The vins doux naturels of Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau are made by mutage, grape spirit added during fermentation to leave natural sugar. Tavel is a rosé of short maceration or saignée, deeper than Provence; Clairette de Die finishes its single fermentation in bottle by the ancestral method, and Saint-Péray and Crémant de Die use the traditional one.

places.name: Northern Rhône
places.note: The steep corridor from Vienne to Valence: Syrah alone for red, Viognier at Condrieu, Marsanne and Roussanne elsewhere, with granite under nearly everything.

places.name: Côte-Rôtie
places.note: The roasted slope above Ampuis, split into the Côte Blonde and the Côte Brune: Syrah with up to 20 per cent Viognier in the vat, the most perfumed northern red; Guigal's La Mouline, La Landonne and La Turque are its famous single vineyards.

places.name: Condrieu
places.note: Viognier only, nearly always dry, from granite terraces just south of Côte-Rôtie: apricot, honeysuckle and oil, for drinking young.

places.name: Château-Grillet
places.note: A single estate with its own appellation inside the Condrieu zone, Viognier from an amphitheatre of granite; one of France's smallest appellations.

places.name: Saint-Joseph
places.note: A long west-bank strip from Condrieu to Cornas, its heart around Mauves and Tournon: Syrah with up to 10 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne, lighter and earlier than Hermitage, plus white.

places.name: Crozes-Hermitage
places.note: The largest northern appellation, on flatter alluvial land around the hill: approachable Syrah with up to 15 per cent white, and the valley's best value, with Marsanne-led whites.

places.name: Hermitage
places.note: One hill behind Tain-l'Hermitage on the east bank, granite at its western end, its lieux-dits Les Bessards, Le Méal and L'Hermite: Syrah of power and decades of life with up to 15 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne, a great white, and vin de paille.

places.name: Cornas
places.note: A warm granite amphitheatre on the west bank: Syrah alone, red alone, dark and rugged, the one northern cru that admits no white grape.

places.name: Saint-Péray
places.note: The southern end of the north: Marsanne and Roussanne, still and traditional method sparkling.

places.name: Diois
places.note: Up the Drôme: Clairette de Die by the ancestral method, Muscat-led and gently sweet; Crémant de Die led by Clairette; Châtillon-en-Diois for still wine.

places.name: Southern Rhône
places.note: From Montélimar to Avignon and across the river to the Gard: Mediterranean, mistral-swept, Grenache-led blends on galets, sand and limestone, with the crus ringing the Dentelles and the papal city.

places.name: Côtes du Rhône and Côtes du Rhône Villages
places.note: The base of the ladder, almost all of it southern; Villages adds lower yields and more Grenache, and a listed commune may put its name on the label.

places.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
places.note: The papal village north of Avignon, whose growers wrote the first modern appellation rules in 1923 and were among the first appellations of 1936: thirteen named grapes, eighteen with colour variants, Grenache leading; red and white, no rosé; the embossed bottle with the papal keys.

places.name: La Crau
places.note: The high plateau of galets roulés east of the village, the stony heartland of the appellation.

places.name: Gigondas
places.note: Under the Dentelles de Montmirail on limestone scree, a cru since 1971: Grenache-led red of depth, a little rosé, and white from the 2023 vintage, Clairette at least 70 per cent, approved by the INAO in September 2022.

places.name: Vacqueyras
places.note: Gigondas's neighbour on lower, warmer ground, a cru since 1990: red, white and rosé, the red Grenache-led and slightly rounder.

places.name: Beaumes-de-Venise
places.note: Both a red cru, since 2005, and the home of Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, the sweet fortified Muscat; the Domaine de Durban makes both.

places.name: Rasteau
places.note: Grenache vin doux naturel in several styles, rancio among them, since 1944, and a cru for dry red since 2010.

places.name: Cairanne
places.note: A cru from the 2015 vintage, red and white, the most recent promotion before Laudun; supple, spicy Grenache blends.

places.name: Vinsobres
places.note: The northernmost southern cru, in the Drôme, red only, promoted in 2006; Syrah plays a larger part here.

places.name: Lirac
places.note: On the west bank in the Gard, Tavel's neighbour: red, white and rosé, the reds in the Châteauneuf mould at a fraction of the price.

places.name: Tavel
places.note: Rosé and nothing else: Grenache and Cinsault with friends, deep in colour, dry, full and made for the table.

places.name: Laudun
places.note: Promoted to cru by the INAO on 11 September 2024 for the 2024 vintage, on the west bank in the Gard: red and white only, with a white share near a third, large for the south.

places.name: Ventoux, Luberon and Costières de Nîmes
places.note: The satellites: Ventoux on the mountain's cooler slopes, Luberon to the south, Costières de Nîmes across the Gard towards the Camargue; Grenache blends in all three colours.

places.name: Grignan-les-Adhémar
places.note: The old Coteaux du Tricastin, renamed in 2010, between the two zones in the Drôme.

producers.name: Domaine Auguste Clape

producers.name: Domaine Jamet

producers.name: Domaine René Rostaing

producers.name: Domaine Georges Vernay

producers.name: Domaine Alain Graillot

producers.name: Château-Grillet

producers.name: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe

producers.name: Domaine du Pégaü

producers.name: Clos des Papes
producers.why: Châteauneuf blended across many parcels in both colours, with a famous white.

producers.name: Henri Bonneau

producers.name: Château de Saint Cosme

producers.name: Domaine Raspail-Ay

terroir.climate: Continental in the north, with cold winters, warm summers and vintage swings; Mediterranean in the south, hot, dry and sunny, with most rain in autumn storms. The mistral blows down the whole valley, cold and dry, drying canopies, cutting rot and stressing the vines.
terroir.soils: Granite, gneiss and schist in the north, weathered to thin sandy soils on terraces; the Côte Brune of Côte-Rôtie holds iron-rich schist, the Côte Blonde lighter granite and gneiss. The south mixes the galets roulés of Châteauneuf, river-rounded quartzite stones over red clay, with sand, limestone scree under the Dentelles de Montmirail and gravel.
terroir.topography: The north is a narrow corridor of terraces cut into slopes so steep that dry-stone walls hold the soil and each vine may be tied to its own stake; Hermitage is a single hill on the east bank, granite at its core. The south opens into a broad plain and low hills, with the jagged limestone Dentelles above Gigondas and Mont Ventoux to the east.
terroir.water: The Rhône itself, whose ancient bed left the galets on the plateau of La Crau; the Isère at the edge of Crozes-Hermitage, the Drôme in the Diois, the Ouvèze below Gigondas and the Durance in the Luberon.

traps: Cornas admits no white grape; Côte-Rôtie may co-ferment Viognier.
Château-Grillet is a single estate with its own appellation inside Condrieu.
Crozes-Hermitage is the largest northern appellation, not a lesser part of Hermitage.
Tavel makes no red or white; its whole appellation is rosé.
The white grapes go into the vat with Syrah; blending finished wines afterwards is not allowed.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape makes red and white but no rosé.
Hermitage Blanc exists and ages for decades; Cornas Blanc does not exist.
Côtes du Rhône is legally both zones, but nearly all of it is southern.
